en: The Proof of Momentary Destruction.
Homage to Samantabhadra!
Pervasion in the form of positive concomitance (anvaya) is that which implies the exclusion of the contrary (vyatireka).
In this context, the presence of the reason in the similar instance (sādharmyavat-dṛṣṭānta) is stated.
Whatever exists is momentary, just like a jar; and these entities under dispute exist.
The capacity of a logical reason (*hetu*) to establish an imperceptible object cannot be demonstrated without first refuting the suspicion that it might be a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Fallacious reasons are of three types, distinguished as unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
In this regard, first of all, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Even if it is true that in every instance of perception various kinds of characteristics of existence have been described, such as the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), [the reason remains established].
Existence is inherence in being, existence by its own nature,
the state of being endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence, and being an object of valid cognition.

[The opponent may argue that] being the object of the means of valid cognition consisting in the apprehension of existence, being the referent of verbal designation, and so forth [constitute existence];
nevertheless, what is the use of this irrelevant matter being determined right now?
For it is precisely that which, when examined through the means of valid cognition, will prove to be the established existence of entities.
We, too, shall accept that very point. However, it is this capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), which is well-known to all people,
that is intended here by the word "existence" (*sattva*) and employed as the means of proof.

And since that [reason] is perceived through a means of valid cognition such as direct perception when things whose existence is established by the means of valid cognition— namely direct perception and inference— are made the subject (*pakṣa*), it is not contradictory either in its own nature or by way of its locus;
for it exists in the pot, which has been made the similar instance (*sapakṣa*).
But how can this [subject] be a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), since, just as with the subject (*pakṣa*), momentary destruction is not established here either?
For its momentary destruction is certainly not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because there is no certainty regarding its being such;
nor is it [established] through inference from existence,
because that would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress due to the requirement of further supporting examples.
And there is no other inference [that could establish momentary destruction].

If it is argued that, should such an inference exist, the proof of momentary destruction would already be established by that very means even for the subject (*pakṣa*), so that the inference from existence (*sattā*) is redundant—[we reply:
it is said:

There exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), which establishes the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) of the jar;
namely: the jar performs a certain purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in the present moment. Would it then perform that same purposeful action in the past and future moments, or another?
"Therefore, one does not perform any action whatsoever"—thus there are three positions.
Of these, the first position is not tenable, because it is impossible to perform what has already been performed.
Now, if the second [position] is accepted, then let this be investigated here:
When a jar performs an effect belonging to the present moment, is it then capable or incapable of performing effects belonging to past and future moments as well?

If it is capable, then it should produce even the effects belonging to past and future moments, just like the effect belonging to the present moment, because it is equally capable with respect to them; for that which is capable cannot be delayed.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its not producing even the effect belonging to the present moment, since there is no distinction between its state of capability in prior and subsequent times.
Furthermore, it is illogical for that which is capable to depend upon auxiliary causes.

If, on the other hand, it were incapable, then—due to the imposition of the contradictory properties of being capable and incapable with respect to a single effect—the momentary destruction of the jar would become unavoidable.
Nor does the third position hold together, because it entails the persistence of a nature that is inherently capable.
For when even a delay in the operation of a potent nature is intolerable, then non-production is cast far away;
otherwise, there would be a non-production of even a present effect, as has been stated.
Therefore, whatever is at whatever time a fit object for the conventional designation of "producing," [it must produce].

At that time, it would perform that [action]; and by not performing it, it would not be subject to the conventional designation of "producing. Thus, because there is a difference at every moment due to having a nature that is either capable or incapable with respect to a single effect, the pot's status as a similar instance (sapakṣa) remains unimpaired.
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Whatever is at any given time capable of the conventional designation of "producing" something, that necessarily produces it at that time;
for example, the final causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) produces its own effect.

Furthermore, this pot is capable of the conventional usage of producing an effect existing in past and future moments even at the time of performing an effect existing in the present moment, and even at the time of transcending all [present] activity; thus, there is a *prasaṅga* based on an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Since this *prasaṅgasādhana*—which has as its object the state of being within the scope of the conventional usage of performing effects existing in the second and subsequent moments—is established for the subject (*dharmin*), namely the pot, at both the time of performing a present effect and the time of transcending all activity, by mere admission of the opponent, non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is certainly impossible.
Nor is there contradiction, because its presence is possible in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), namely in the final causal complex (*antyakāraṇasāmagrī*).
[Objection: But is this not a common inconclusive reason (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika-hetu*)?

If it is argued that [the reason] is observed even in a non-producer—such as a seed situated in a granary and so forth, which belongs to the class of counter-examples (vipakṣa)—because it falls within the scope of the conventional usage "capable," we say: no.
For the conventional usage "capable" is of two kinds: ultimate (pāramārthika) and figurative (aupacārika).
Of these, that which is ultimate—the state of being the object of the convention "producer" as necessitated by actual production—is what is employed here as the probans (sādhana).

Furthermore, since seeds and the like situated in a granary or similar storage are merely the causes of causes—and thus subjects of the figurative convention of "production"—the [probandum] cannot possibly exist there; how, then, could there be the fallacy of inconclusiveness due to commonality?
Nor is there any doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because there exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary.
For it is established by the experience of all people that this state of being the object of the convention of "production" is pervaded by having a restricted scope.
And this [arising] is not without a cause,
for that would entail the consequence of there being no restriction regarding place, time, or intrinsic nature;
nor is any cause other than production perceived.
This is because we observe that [the effect] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of that [cause].

Furthermore, if the status of being an object of the conventional usage "production" were possible even in the absence of actual production, then there would be no restriction, and the conventional usage of "production" would apply to everything everywhere;
yet this [usage] is observed to be restricted.

Therefore, since the pervader—namely, having a restricted object—absent in the counter-example (vipakṣa) where there is no production, ceases to exist, the status of being an object of the conventional usage "production" must rest solely upon actual production; thus, because the pervasion is established, the reason is faultless.
Furthermore, this jar does not produce an effect belonging to past or future moments either during the present moment of performing its function or when it has transcended all activity.
Therefore, it is not fit for the conventional usage of "production.
This is because of the logical principle that every reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) must culminate in its contradictory (prasaṅgaviparyaya).
Here too, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:

Whatever does not produce a certain effect at a certain time is, at that time and in that respect, incapable of being conventionally designated as "capable," just as *kodrava* grain is incapable with respect to the production of a rice sprout.

This jar does not produce the effect belonging to the present moment—namely, the act of producing—at the time of performing that function, nor does it produce the effects belonging to past and future moments at the time of transcending all such activity; thus, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) excludes [its capacity].
From a moment that is capable [of producing an effect], there arises a moment that is incapable.

Here too, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because it is impossible for an effect belonging to a past or future moment to be produced at the time when the effect belonging to the present moment is being produced, or at the time when all activity has ceased.
Nor is there any contradiction (*virodha*), because [the reason] exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Nor is there any inconclusiveness, because, by the reasoning previously stated, the pervasion between being capable and producing an object within the scope of linguistic convention—both of which are positive entities—has been established as encompassing all cases.
Furthermore, regarding what was said here: "If something does not produce something at a certain time, it is not capable of that at that time"—in this context, what is the meaning of "producing"?
Is it causality?
Is it the completeness of auxiliary conditions conducive to the production of that effect, or rather the non-deviation from the effect,
or perhaps the connection with the effect?
In this context, the very state of being a cause (*kāraṇatva*) is the meaning of "acting" (*karoti*).
Consequently, the faults that might arise from alternative positions are neutralized by the fact that those positions are not accepted.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to assert here—on the grounds that "being a cause" and "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) are synonyms—that the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*).

Since the probandum is the absence of being the object of the convention "capable," and since there is a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) between "causality" and "being the object of the convention 'capable'"— just as there is between "tree" and "śiṃśapā"— there is no occasion at all for such petty prattle.
Thus, by the force of both the reason of the reductio (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established in the example of a jar.

How then can it be said that there is no inference other than existence (*sattva*) that establishes momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) in the example? Nor, in this way, is the reason of existence rendered useless.

Since the proof of momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established through both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*) by means of the mere example alone, one might object: "In that case, let the establishment of momentariness in the subject (*pakṣa*) also proceed from these two [arguments] themselves.
Let it be so; what is the fault?

For a cognizer who is not too lazy to set forth the argument for every individual thing—that "whatever is capable of the activity of producing something at a certain time, produces it at that time," and so forth—for such a person, the establishment of momentariness follows from that very [argument].

However, one who is afraid of the effort involved in applying that logic to every individual object may, by means of a single substratum (*dharmī*), ascertain that mere existence is pervaded by non-stability through such a principle as: "Whatever is at any time capable of being designated as producing something, that produces it at that time," and thereby understands momentariness in other cases simply from the fact of existence.

How could one who is not negligent declare this [existence] to be futile? Thus, in the case of a jar which performs a single function, there is indeed a difference [between its states] due to the superimposition of contradictory properties—namely, being capable or otherwise—relative to the effects occurring in the second and subsequent moments. Therefore, when the reason "existence" is perceived in a jar that possesses momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), it does not constitute a contradiction with the subject.

Nor is this [reason] inconclusive, because the pervasion—characterized by a comprehensive inclusion (sarvopasaṃhāravatī)—has been established within this very example possessing the same properties (sādharmyavat).

If it is objected: "The establishment of pervasion occurs through the force of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) regarding the opposite case, yet there is not even a mention of such a presentation; how then has the pervasion been established? [the reply follows:]...
This is merely a play of a most flickering intellect;

for it has been stated that since a jar possesses the capacity to produce effects belonging to past and future moments at the very time it is performing the action of its present moment, it would follow that at that same time it is both capable and incapable by nature, depending on whether it produces or does not produce those [past and future] effects.
The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāśakti*) is necessarily pervaded by momentariness, insofar as it involves change at every moment.
If it is asked, "In that case, let there be mere positive concomitance (*anvaya*); how is the absolute exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) obtained?
[the answer is: precisely because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established.

If it is asked, "How is the establishment of pervasion (vyāpti) possible when there is doubt regarding negative concomitance (vyatireka)?"—the answer is no; for the establishment of pervasion is twofold: that which consists of positive concomitance (anvaya), which is a property of the agent [the prover], namely, the necessary presence of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) in a subject (dharmin) that possesses the proving property (sādhanadharma).
And the negative form is the property of the action (*karmadharma*), which is the necessary absence of the means (*sādhana*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent.
Of these two, the cognition of either one necessarily implies the cognition of the second;
otherwise, only one would be established.
Therefore,

just as when the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established as being invariably certain by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) regarding the contrary case, the doubt previously situated regarding the domain of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) subsequently vanishes;
consequently, no separate proof is stated for the purpose of establishing that positive concomitance.

Thus, when a necessary positive concomitance (anvaya) is established by the force of both the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and its converse (tadviparyaya), the doubt that previously existed regarding the domain of negative concomitance (vyatireka) subsequently dissolves entirely.
Furthermore, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) need be stated to establish that negative concomitance;
consequently, there is an absolute absence of the probans (sādhana) wherever the probandum (sādhya) is absent.

When the means of proof exists, there is necessarily a concomitance with that which is to be proven; thus, there is no difference in meaning. Therefore, even without a subverting proof against the contrary, since the pervasion in the form of positive concomitance is established by the force of both the reductio (*prasaṅga*) and the reason of the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*), the reason "existence" (*sattva*) is not inconclusive. Consequently, the establishment of momentary destruction from this means of proof is faultless.
But is this proof not unestablished?
For an effect is not apprehended by means of the cognition of its cause,
because it is yet to come into being.
Nor can the cause be apprehended by means of the cognition of the effect,
because that [the cause] has already passed away.
Furthermore, an object that is past or future cannot be grasped by a cognition that perceives only the present, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, there is no single reconnecting subject (*pratisandhātṛ*) between the earlier and later moments, as that would entail the collapse of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Moreover, for one who maintains the theory of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the realization of the absence of an effect due to the absence of a cause is beyond even the reach of their imagination.

Nor is it logical to claim that there are two cognitions at the earlier and later times, that from these two arises a latent impression (*vāsanā*), and that from that impression arises a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which determines the relationship of cause and effect.
For that conceptual construction (vikalpa) must either be one that connects what has been grasped or one that superimposes a form that does not belong to it; the first alternative is not tenable,
because in the absence of a single unifier, the grasping of the preceding and the subsequent would be impossible,
as there would be no latent impression (vāsanā) for conceptual construction at all.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for it would entail the consequence that even the cognition of water in a mirage would be valid.
Thus, since neither positive nor negative concomitance is established, existence characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) remains unproven.
Furthermore, this proof is unestablished for another reason as well.
For instance, the capacity of seeds and so forth must be determined either from the cognition of the seed and so forth, or from the effect, such as the sprout.
And the status of being an effect is established only upon the establishment of its being a real entity (vastu).
And its being a real entity [is established] through another effect;
the status of that other effect as an effect is established upon the proof of its being a real entity;
and that reality of it, in turn, [depends] on yet another subsequent effect—thus there is an infinite regress.

Now, if—out of fear of an infinite regress—one does not require another effect at the final limit, then by that very fact it follows that the preceding [causes] would lack existence; thus, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is not established even for a single thing.
But surely, the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) of "being an effect" and "existence" are distinct?
If it is argued that even if existence (*sattva*) is established, what harm is there if the state of being an effect (*kāryyatva*) is also established? That is inconsistent;

for even though there is a difference in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) between the state of being an effect and existence, how can the establishment of the state of being an effect follow from the establishment of existence?

For being an effect (kāryyatva) is indeed the state of coming into existence after not having existed; and coming into existence is being (sattā); and for the Sugatas, being is nothing other than causal capacity (sāmarthya).

Furthermore, when there is doubt regarding its capacity (*sāmarthya*), it is impossible even to say "it exists"; how then can "being produced after not having existed" (*abhūtvābhāvitva*)—which is the definition of being an effect (*kāryatva*)—be established?

Even the definition that "being an effect consists in depending on the operation of another" is not a property of a non-existent thing. Existence (*sattva*) is capacity (*sāmarthya*), and since that is doubtful, how can the status of being an effect be proven?
If that is not proven, the capacity of the former [reason] is not established; thus, the reason is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).

Likewise, this [position] is also contradictory; for if things were momentary, it would not be possible for that which is unarisen or that which has ceased without leaving a trace to initiate an effect.
Nor does that which has already been produced possess even such a moment as could be employed for the sake of some effect.

Therefore, in the case of momentariness alone, there is a contradiction because purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is untenable. Alternatively, whatever is presented by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), all that is non-substantial (*avastu*).
Furthermore, when momentariness—which is of the nature of a real entity—is to be proven, an inferential conceptualization that posits a non-entity is contradictory.

Alternatively, for every reason (hetu) when momentariness is to be proven, there is contradiction: if it does not persist across different places and times, the relationship between the probandum and the probans (sādhyasādhanabhāva) is absent; and if it does persist, then a single entity existing at various times would be non-momentary, which contradicts momentariness.
"This [reason] is also inconclusive, because there is no contradiction between existence and stability.
To this it is said: as for what was stated, that "the capacity is not perceived,"...
Is it then the case that nothing at all is perceived, or is this [non-perception] only under the view of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)?

In the first case, because the entire cycle of causes— both those that produce and those that indicate— would be annihilated, it would follow as an absurd consequence that one could not even perform the mere movement of the face.

Otherwise, the very statement by which it is established that there is no capacity would itself arrive at the unimpeded capacity to establish that [very absence]. Therefore, for one who is engaged in the investigation of the reality of things with the desire for the supreme human goal, activity must be preceded by the acceptance of causal capacity. If that were not accepted, no one would engage in anything anywhere, and the world would become devoid of all activity.
Now, as for the second position:
there is, at least, the cognition of capacity;
and if that is not possible given momentariness, then it is appropriate to state a contradiction.
The claim that "this is not established" is, for the most part, merely the lamentation of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*.
Furthermore, even if momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) were true, there would be no contradiction in the cognition of causal capacity.

To explain: by means of a cognition apprehending the effect—which is the product of the cognition of the cause and which contains within it the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by that [cause]—the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is produced in the form: "When this exists, that exists."

Likewise, with respect to the cause, by means of the cognition apprehending the isolation of the ground—which is the effect produced by that [cognition]—and with respect to the effect, by means of the cognition apprehending the isolation of the ground which contains within it the latent impression deposited by that [cause], the determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is produced in the form: "In the absence of this, there is the absence of that.
As the Teachers have said:
A subsequent cognition, arising immediately after the single determination, establishes an inferential reflection;
thus, through the experience of the absence of that one [object], it generates a cognition of exclusion and brings forth the notion of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
This being the case, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is one that synthesizes what has been previously apprehended;
for it is a synthesis of two successive perceptions that have apprehended the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). As the *Alaṃkāra* states:

If indeed a single perception does not possess the cognition of both the preceding and the succeeding [moments], then how can there be the cognition of the prior and the posterior when two perceptions exist? Nor is the second alternative [the existence of a single, enduring cognizer] tenable, as it would entail the flaw of [postulating] a permanent self.
For the Buddhists maintain this position: "existence" (sattva) is indeed "efficacy" (sāmarthya).
Nor is this our undertaking begun now merely for the sake of proving that;

rather, it is for the purpose of establishing momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) in those cases where there is a subject (dharmin) such as a seed, which is a real entity established by valid cognition (pramāṇa), and wherein efficacy is also established by valid cognition.

Therefore, although there may be doubt regarding the capacity [of seeds] because the effect, such as the sprout, is not yet perceived, its mere existence (*sanmātratva*)—established by clear perception—must certainly be acknowledged.
Otherwise, there would be no apprehension of even a mere entity anywhere.

Thus, even when there is doubt regarding the definition of existence according to the scriptures, the fact that the state of being an effect is observed in the sprout and so forth—which is supported by the force of clear perception—establishes the capacity of the seed and other causes.
There is no room for the fault of contradiction;
nor is there any loss of causal capacity in the case of momentariness, from which a contradiction might arise.
There is no contradiction between the two definitions of causality— namely, momentariness and the state of being necessarily antecedent—
because causal capacity is possible even in that which lasts for only a single moment; thus, the first contradiction does not exist,
nor does the second variety of contradiction.

Even if the own-form (*svākāra*)—whether it be a non-entity or an entity—is what is apprehended, since validity is established in all cases only with respect to the object that is determined (*adhyavaseya*), the momentariness of the very nature of the real entity (*vastu-svabhāva*) is proven; so where is the contradiction?

If it is argued: "Both that which is apprehended and that which is determined are merely the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) and not real entities, because if they were to penetrate the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the association with verbal expression would be impossible"—we say: no.

Because its essential nature as determination (*adhyavasāya*) is not understood, the determinative character of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists in its capacity to cause mental activity and the like even with respect to an object that has not been grasped; and the state of being determined (*adhyavaseyatva*) consists in being made the object of such activity despite not appearing [in the cognition].
And this state of being determined is applicable only to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and not to anything else.
Because the activity of the seeker is directed toward purposeful efficacy (*arthakriyā*),
when there is such a determination (*adhyavasāya*), the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not indeed appear [in that determination].
Nor does it follow that, even though it does not appear, there would be the undesirable consequence of prompting activity everywhere without distinction.
Because it is produced from a specific causal complex,
because it possesses its own specific form,
and because it is endowed with a specific capacity.
[The causal capacity] is indeed restricted [to its specific effect], because even when that which is not of that nature has been excluded is not perceived, one observes the efficacy of the activity;

just as, despite the non-existence of everything else, it is observed that a sprout arises only from a seed, for it is impossible to reject the established relation of cause and effect. However, the distinction is this: validity exists when there is a connection with an external object, whereas invalidity exists otherwise.
Likewise, the third position is also fruitless in its effort;

for even though a single entity existing at various times is impossible in reality, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans—which are merely the exclusion of what is not of that nature—is grasped by perception.

Indeed, the object of perception is twofold: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). Let it be that the mere thing, which is entirely excluded from what is not of that nature, does not become the apprehended object of perception because it does not manifest directly.

However, when a portion of that [object] is apprehended, because it generates a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that ascertains the pervasion between those two [the part and the whole], the object certainly becomes one that is determined (*adhyavaseya*).
This is like the ascertainment of a continuum upon the apprehension of a single moment,
or like the ascertainment of a jar upon the apprehension of its mere color-form (*rūpa*).
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.
For instance, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs either between two universals or between two particulars.
The alternatives are: either [the cognition] of the universal qualified by the particular, or of the particular qualified by the universal.
It is not the first alternative, because the universal is sublated; and even if it were not sublated, it would be imperceptible.
Even though it is perceptible, it cannot be inferred because it is not conducive to human goals; nor can there be an inference of a particular from an inferred universal, because—
according to the reasoning to be stated later— it is impossible to apprehend the necessary connection (pratibandha) between a universal and all its particulars.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because a particular (viśeṣa) cannot be concomitant [with others].
Regarding the final two alternatives, the particular must either be made the qualified or the qualifier of the universal (sāmānya), being perceived as the very substratum of that universal;
or else it must be something unperceived, existing in another place or time.
Alternatively, every particular (*viśeṣa*)—consisting of both the perceived and the unperceived, existing in other places and times, and excluded from what is not of that nature—is [the object].
The first position is not tenable because it lacks universal concomitance (*ananugāmitva*);
nor is the second.
Because it has not been seen.
Nor is it the third [alternative],
because even when one specific instance is observed, those existing in other places and times remain unseen.
Now, because all these particularities (*viśeṣa*) are similar—

due to being produced by a similar causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and due to performing a similar function— it is through this proximity that perception, which grasps a single particularity, generates a determination based merely on the exclusion of what is not of that nature (*atadrūpaparāvṛtta*); thus, it establishes merely the particularity as excluded from what is not of that nature.
Just as perception, which grasps only that form obstructed by a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), is established as "grasping the jar" when it produces a determination regarding a jar;
otherwise, neither the jar nor even the continuum of the jar would be established through perception, because there is no grasping of it in its entirety.
Furthermore, the grasping of a single part is no different even in the case of [an object] excluded from what does not possess that nature.

If this is so, then let the comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) for every particular instance also occur in this very same manner, just as there is the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

Why, then, should it be accepted that [the object] exists at different times or is momentary, such that the probans (*sādhana*) would be contradictory in the case of momentariness? Thus, there is no possibility of any such distinction of contradiction. Nor is this reason (*hetu*) inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Because, according to the sequence previously stated, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) form of pervasion is established in the homogeneous example (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*) by means of both the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its contrapositive (*viparyaya*).

Now, it is indeed logical that if momentary destruction were established in the example of a jar through the force of these two reasons— the reductio and its contrapositive— then, since the pervasion of existence by momentariness would be established as a rule, there could be no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).
This alone is impossible;
for even a pot that is capable will produce its effects sequentially by depending on sequential auxiliary causes.
Nor should it be said that a capable entity acts solely by virtue of its own intrinsic nature.
Since its own nature (svarūpa) exists at all times, dependence upon an auxiliary cause (sahakārī), which provides no further assistance, is not logical.
Even if it possesses causal agency by virtue of its own nature, how can it produce an effect if it lacks efficacy (sāmarthya)?
For efficacy consists in the completeness of auxiliary causes, while the lack thereof constitutes a lack of efficacy.
Furthermore, there is no impairment whatsoever of that which possesses those two [properties] due to their appearance and disappearance,
because it is distinct from them.
Therefore, since it is possible for an object to be capable yet not act, the probans in this reductio (*prasaṅga*) has a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*).
To this it is replied: Let it be granted for now that capacity (*sāmarthya*) is simply the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārisākalya*).

Even so, that entity (*bhāva*) must first of all be an agent by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Now, if its very same nature—which in the final moment possesses the property of non-delayed action—were present in the first moment as well, then it would necessarily act even at that time, and could not be prevented even by Brahmā.
Furthermore, even that nature which possesses the property of non-delayed action cannot be said to be distinct from the entity when it has arisen in its entirety;
for otherwise, it would follow that the entity itself is a non-agent.
Thus, to whatever extent other properties are conceptually constructed, to that same extent the entity remains indifferent [to them].
Therefore, regarding that nature which it is said to produce even by its own essence,

if that [nature] existed even previously, how could there ever be non-production? If the prior state, whose nature is opposed to non-delayed action, persists later on, how could the effect ever possibly come into being?

Now, if that [single cause] alone were the agent, this would indeed be logical. However, since it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces [the effect], then at a time when other auxiliary factors are absent, the effect is not produced even by that which is most powerful; what contradiction is there in this?
For a thing does not produce [an effect] by its own nature simply because it is its own nature; rather, it produces [it] precisely through its own nature [as part of a complex].
Since it is observed that the production of an effect occurs only from that [cause] when accompanied by auxiliary factors,

therefore, like pervasion (*vyāpti*), the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) must also be understood in one case through the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*), and in the other case through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
"In the same way, because there is agreement among worldly investigators.

To this it is replied: When things, being conjoined, perform an effect, let their "cooperation" (sahakāritva) consist in the characteristic of performing a single purpose; who can deny that? But from where is it obtained that the effect must be produced by those [causes] alone when they are conjoined?
Because an entity possesses a single nature throughout its prior and subsequent states,
it is impossible to avoid the unavoidable consequence that it must be restricted to either always producing or never producing.

Therefore, the claim that "the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the producer, not a single [entity] which is the producer" lies beyond the reach of even the wildest dreams of those who maintain the doctrine of permanence.

If it is argued that "it is indeed seen to be thus," let it be seen; however, the point of contention is whether the production of an effect arises from a thing already present that has entered into the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or rather from a distinct thing produced [subsequently]. In this regard, if [the cause] were possible even previously, the effect would either be produced at all times or never at all; yet, without resolving this contradiction, one merely repeats the thesis, closing one's eyes and saying, "Because the production of the effect is seen from that very [cause]."
It is said that [the self] deserves compassion;

yet, oneness cannot be established through the force of recognition and the like, because such [recognition] is found even in the case of hair and nails that have been cut off and grown back again— thereby undermining its reliability— and because it is impossible to demonstrate any difference in their characteristics.
Since this has already been refuted by us in detail in the *Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa*, [we need not elaborate further].
Therefore, with respect to the direct relationship of cause and effect, there is an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) in both cases.

However, in the case of pervasion (*vyāpti*), with respect to the cause in its entirety—whether directly or indirectly—there is an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) regarding the pervading cause.
When the effect (*kāryya*) is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), there is the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).

Likewise, when that which is not of its nature (*tadatatsvabhāva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*), there is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). And when that which is of its nature (*tatsvabhāva*) is the pervaded, there is the exclusion of connection with anything else; thus, with respect to pervasion as it appears in conceptual construction (*vikalpāruḍharūpa*), there are two kinds of restriction.

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "If an entity were observed to possess a single nature across earlier and later times, and were thus pervaded by either always being a producer or always being a non-producer, then this reductio ad absurdum would be consistent.
However, for the proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*), no single entity whatsoever is observed across earlier and later times.
To this we reply: this is extremely crude.
For instance, the meaning of the phrase "given that there is a single nature at the earlier and later times" is as follows:
if that very nature of an entity which exists at a later time and is productive were also to exist at the earlier time;
or if that very nature which exists at the earlier time and is non-productive were also to exist at the later time.
In that case, production or non-production would be nothing other than what is already perceived;

and this being so, since one is merely superimposing identity upon two established natures, it follows that production or non-production—which are themselves already established—is what is attributed.
[Objection: But surely it is the effect itself that depends upon auxiliary causes?

But it is not the cause for the production of the effect. For capacity is of two kinds: innate and adventitious. Since there are other auxiliary causes, even for a non-momentary entity, a variety of effects can arise sequentially due to the diversity of sequential auxiliaries; thus, if it is argued that it is impossible to establish the moment-by-moment difference between entities— [The response follows: ... [this argument is refuted by the fact that] even if the capacity is present, the non-momentary entity cannot produce its effects sequentially because it lacks the necessary sequential variation in its causal conditions. Therefore, the necessity of momentariness remains unrefuted.
It is said:
Let it be granted for now that capacity is twofold, distinguished as innate and adventitious;

nevertheless, regarding that specific individual characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a thing—which must necessarily be admitted to possess the property of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—the refutation that was previously uttered by means of the dilemma as to whether it exists prior [to the effect] or only subsequently, [remains to be addressed].
In this regard, we do not understand what has been stated by him. As for the argument that "the auxiliary causes are required precisely because of the effect," that too is useless;
for if the effect itself were independent in its own production, then that [argument] would be correct.
This being the case, the postulation of the capacity of the completeness of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-sākalya*) is fruitless;
for the effect will occur only occasionally by virtue of [the cause's] very independence.
And this being so, the existing causes would be entirely incapable.
The pure understanding [concludes] that this effect is independent.
Now, if it is argued that this is simply the fault of the effect itself—that it sometimes does not arise even when a capable cause exists—[we reply:
then, because of its independence, it is not truly an effect of that [cause].
As for the commentary:
"If, even when the cause is the same across all states, there were non-production of the effect, then the effect would be independent; such being the case, it would not be an effect."

Now, if it is argued that something is called an "effect" not because it exists when that [cause] exists, but rather because it necessarily exists only through the absence of that [cause], on account of the predominance of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); we say no.
For if the cause, by its own nature, were to produce its effect, then there would be the cognition that "its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that [cause]."
If it is argued that, even when the cause exists, the effect does not arise due to its own independence,
then by what could the doubt be dispelled that, likewise, even in the absence of that cause, it might not have arisen precisely because of its independence?
As the Bhāṣya states:
If it does not exist even when that [cause] exists, how can it be non-existent when that is absent? How can it be said that its non-existence is necessitated by the non-existence of that?
Therefore, just as it does not necessarily arise when that [cause] is present,
so too it would necessarily arise when that [cause] is absent;
yet since it does not so arise, it cannot admit of itself being the cause of that [effect].
As for what was said— that at the time of producing the first effect, it possesses the nature of producing subsequent effects,
and therefore it should produce all effects at that very first moment—
this is improper because it contradicts its own statement, like saying, "My mother is barren."
How could that which has the nature of producing an effect at a later time produce that effect at the beginning?
If it does not, then it does not have the nature of producing that effect; for indeed, that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth.
To this it is replied: if an entity possesses a stable nature, why is it that this effect occurs only at a later time and not at an earlier time?
And because of that absence, how can the cause also have the nature of producing a subsequent effect?
What can we do? If it is argued that its birth occurs only at a later time, let it be so; however, since that is impossible for something stable, let it point toward instability.
If it is argued that even while remaining [in that state], this very same nature belongs to it such that it acts only at the subsequent moment,
then what hope is there for any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For even in the case of "fire from smoke," one could equally say that its very nature is such that smoke might exist here now even without fire.
Therefore, there is reliance upon intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because it is established by valid cognition (pramāṇa),
but the subversion of valid cognition does not occur through reliance upon intrinsic nature.
Consequently, if one were to assert that an effect exists in its first moment by accepting that a cause produces a subsequent effect, [it would lead to an absurdity].
There would be a contradiction with one's own words;
for when the cause is permanent, it is logically inconsistent for the effect to exist at a later time.
Therefore, since the production of a subsequent effect by a cause is in fact impossible, this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (a reductio ad absurdum).
It has been established that being the object of the conventional usage "producing" is pervaded by the act of producing.

Furthermore, since you yourself accept it, the state of being the object of the conventional usage "producing a subsequent effect" is established in the subject—the jar—at the very time it performs its first action.
Therefore, the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is formulated precisely because a subsequent effect—which is necessarily concomitant with that [act of producing]—is impossible in the first moment.

For even when one attributes the capacity to produce yellow to that which produces blue, there is no logical consequence that yellow must actually arise; this is what is called a contradiction with one's own words.

Thus, being capable is pervaded by producing, because it does not depend on auxiliary causes. And that which does not produce is indeed distinct [from the capable], due to the imposition of the contradictory properties of being capable and incapable.

Now, it may be granted that by the force of the reversal of the *prasaṅga*, there is the imposition of contradictory properties characterized by capacity and incapacity with respect to a single effect. Nevertheless, difference is not established thereby;

for instance, if a seed, while producing a sprout and so forth, were to produce the earth and other factors by the very same nature (*svabhāva*) by which it produces the sprout, then it would follow that the earth and other factors would also possess the nature of a sprout.

If, however, agency were due to having various intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), then because those natures are invariably characterized by mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), existence and non-existence—which are mutually contradictory—would occur in a single locus; thus, even a single seed would be divided.
The same applies to a lamp, which performs the exhaustion of oil, the burning of the wick, and so forth;
likewise, a preceding form (*rūpa*) also produces subsequent forms, tastes, odors, and so on, being itself surrounded by numerous intrinsic natures.
Furthermore, because these intrinsic natures are invariably characterized by mutual non-existence, if contradictory things were to combine, lamps and such would be split apart;
yet they are not split apart.
Therefore, that is not the case.
The superimposition of contradictory properties is what constitutes differentiation;

likewise, a seed’s status as a producer with respect to a sprout and its non-producer status with respect to a donkey and so forth are two contradictory properties of being a producer and not being a producer.
Yet, despite possessing these, there is no difference in the seed itself.

Thus, in this way, the attribution of contradictory properties—such as being capable or incapable—which is observed in the case of the seed, the lamp, and form (rūpa) when they are opposed [to their effects], does not differentiate a jar or similar objects.
To this we reply:

Granted that seeds and the like possess a distinction of multiple intrinsic natures (svabhāva) by virtue of their capacity to produce multiple effects; nevertheless, what relevance has the attribution of contradictory properties here?
For when intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are not deviant from their mutual non-existence, it is difference (*bheda*) that finds its occasion, not contradiction (*virodha*).

Contradiction, however, would exist between two things when the affirmation of one entails the negation of the other, and the negation of one entails the affirmation of the other, by virtue of their existing through mutual exclusion within a single substratum (*dharmī*).
Thus, in this case, it is logical for one intrinsic nature to be contradictory with its own absence, just as existence is contradictory with non-existence.
But it is not by means of another intrinsic nature,
as in the case of pot-ness and substantiality;
likewise, the capacity to produce a sprout and so forth is contradicted by the incapacity to produce that [same effect], but not by the capacity to produce some other thing.
And here, the operation of perception is such that it establishes an entity, though superimposed with various properties, as non-different—
just as it establishes that which performs a certain effect as distinct from that which does not perform that effect.

Thus, if, due to the absence of mutual opposition, two natures are not contradictory even while being invariably concomitant with mutual exclusion, then their respective capacities to produce those effects or to produce other effects are not contradictory either, owing to the difference in their objects.
What, then, follows from this? [There would be] a contradiction between two mutually exclusive properties—capacity and incapacity—with respect to a single effect.
Furthermore, if there were no contradiction even between these two, then contradiction itself would be as good as dead.
Let it be, then, that there is a contradiction between capacity and incapacity only with reference to a single effect.

If it is argued: "Just as with respect to that same effect, power and lack of power are not contradictory due to the difference in location—such that there is power in one place and a lack of power in another place—likewise, power and lack of power are also not contradictory due to the difference in time with respect to the very same effect, just as a crystal was previously inactive and that same [crystal] is subsequently active," we reply: We do not say, based on mere convention, that power and lack of power are not contradictory in a single effect simply because of a difference in location.
However, there is no contradiction [in this case],
because the capacity to perform a function in a particular place and time is indeed contradicted by the incapacity to perform that same function in that same place and time;
it is not, however, contradicted by the incapacity to perform that function in another place, nor by the performance of some other function.
If this is so, then the capacity to perform a function at that specific time is contradictory to the incapacity to perform that same function at that same time;
it is not, however, contradictory to the incapacity to perform that function at another time, nor to the capacity to perform some other function.
If it is asked: "In that case, how can there be contradiction even when the times differ?"
It is said:
For contradiction between two properties, characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion within a single substratum, is a rule of non-coexistence;
and that [contradiction] occurs either through direct mutual opposition, as in the case of existence and non-existence, or [indirectly].

Alternatively, because it is necessarily sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would be like [the properties of] permanence and existence; thus, there is no difference in meaning.

Therefore, in this case, within a single substratum (*dharmin*)—which is the locus of performing that action at that time—there is a contradiction because its non-performance of that action, or its performance of another action, at a different time is necessarily sublated by another means of valid cognition. For instance, in whatever substratum the performance of that action at that time is perceived, even Brahmā could not establish the non-performance of that action or the performance of another action at a different time in that very same substratum.
By this, there would be no contradiction between these two [statements],

because the difference between the subjects (*dharmī*) is necessarily established by means of the reasons consisting in the reversal of the aforementioned reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*) at another moment;
nor is oneness established by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
This is because human agency has been uprooted.

For this very reason, even a diamond (vajra) has been cast aside along with the wings and belly; how then can that wretched crystal serve as an example to prove non-difference despite the difference in time?

Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) among effects produced at the same time, even if they differ in location, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish such difference, and because non-difference is established by sensory perception (*indriyapratyakṣa*), which eliminates any suspicion of error.

Thus, even when there is a difference in time, the contradiction between capacity and incapacity cannot be set aside merely by convention (*samaya*), because neither convention nor authority (*pramāṇa*) applies in such a case. Therefore, in all instances, the establishment of difference is precisely the establishment of the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*).
However, for one who is mistaken, the conventional usage of difference is established through the superimposition of contradictory properties.

But even so, this [reason] "existence" (*sattva*) is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), either because it is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) or because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.
For instance, just as this [existence] is excluded from non-momentary things by the exclusion of succession and simultaneity, [so too is it excluded from the subject].
Likewise, when both pervading properties—dependence and independence, as well as unity and plurality—are excluded from even a momentary entity, [the following occurs]:

for instance, a seed-moment that co-exists with a causal condition such as Devadatta’s hand is held to be produced from its own preceding complex [of causes] as something capable and independent, generating the first excellence [of the series].

In that case, among many seed-series born within the same field, why does only one particular seed produce, through a succession [of moments], what is conducive to the production of a sprout, while other seed-moments do not?

Indeed, prior to the condition of contact (*upasarpaṇapratyaya*), there is no mutual excellence whatsoever among those seed-moments (*bījakṣaṇa*) existing within either a homogeneous or heterogeneous continuum.

Now, prior to contact, even those [moments] belonging to that same continuum do not produce a seed-moment conducive to the production of a sprout through a succession [of causes], because they merely produce seeds.
Only for a certain seed-moment, co-arising with the condition of contact, does there arise the production of an initial excellence.
Well then, in the absence of which [auxiliaries], even that which has already arisen would simply not produce [the effect];

likewise, since deviation is possible for individual factors alone, one must—even against one's will—accept that earth and the other [elements] produce either the initial excellence or the sprout only when they are mutually dependent.
Therefore, independence is not possible for a momentary entity.
Nor is independence (anapekṣā) tenable;

for it is impossible for there to be a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between two moments existing at the same time, just as it is between the left and right horns of a cow. Thus, the first pervading absence [of the reason] is not unestablished (asiddha).

Furthermore, if the final seed-moment, while acting independently to produce the sprout and so forth, produces the earth and other factors by the very same nature by which it produces the sprout, [then they would be identical].
In that case, since earth and the other factors would also possess the nature of the sprout due to having an identical cause, the possibility of [their] being one is not tenable.
[Objection: But it acts by means of a different form;
for instance, the seed has the status of a material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the sprout, whereas earth and the others have the status of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
If this is so, are these two—the state of being a cooperative cause and the state of being the material cause—identical or distinct?
If they are one, how can it be a producer by means of a different form?
If they are distinct, however, is there a difference between these two from the seed, or are they non-different?
If there is difference, how can the seed possess the nature of a producer, since the sprout and so forth arise from those two [the seed and the sprout] themselves?
Or, if there is non-difference, why does the seed not possess multiplicity, given its identity with what is distinct?
Or else, these two must be one, due to their identity as one.
If it should be argued that,
when earth and so forth are to be produced, the material cause of that [earth] is simply a prior transformation of the form of the seed of earth and so forth—
then the seed would not be the producer of earth and so forth independently of those [transformations].
If they were independent of those [conditions], the emergence of the sprout would be impossible;
furthermore, you yourself have stated that things do not depend on what provides no assistance.

Moreover, since no assistance is possible for a momentary entity other than its production—and because that [moment] is indivisible—there is no plurality either. Thus, the second pervader (vyāpaka) is also not established as absent.
Therefore, [the reason] is "inconclusive due to being uncommon" (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), like the property of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*).

If it is thought that even those which provide no assistance are auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) and must be depended upon— because the presence or absence of the effect conforms to them and because they perform the action together—

then, by this same logic, even a non-momentary entity might depend upon successive auxiliary causes that provide no assistance, since their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is replicated in the successive effect.
Furthermore, because effects will be produced in succession by virtue of auxiliary causes acting in sequence, the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is unestablished;
thus, existence (*sattva*) is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to its doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*) regarding the proof of momentariness.
To this we reply:
With reference to what kind of meaning of "dependence" is it stated that for a momentary thing there is the cessation of both dependence and non-dependence?
Does "it depends on an auxiliary cause" mean that an assistance must be rendered to it by that auxiliary cause?
Now, [one might argue that] there is a joint action with the auxiliary cause for the seed and so forth already existing in their prior state;
or else, the meaning of "dependence" (apekṣā) is merely the production of that which was previously existing in a state of non-dependent conjunction.
Here, since the first position is impossible, how can there be the exclusion of both [dependence and non-dependence] for a momentary entity, given that it is indeed independent?
If it is momentary and independent, why does it not act even in the absence of the conditions for its approach?
It would indeed act, if it were so.
But how could that which is inherently incapable act?
Furthermore, there is no distinction between saying "it was such" or "it was like that.
Therefore, even if a nature of that kind were possible, its non-production [of an effect] cannot be tolerated as independence from auxiliary causes. If this is argued:
This is inconsistent;
for even when there is similarity in color and shape, the non-agent lacks that specific nature.

And that specific nature, characterized by the capacity to produce a subsequent excellence, is not possible in all seed-moments existing within either similar or dissimilar continua, but only in certain ones, such as those [seeds] that perform the function [of producing a sprout].
[Objection: "Surely, when all seeds— having been produced and harvested in a single field and then brought together and cast into a single granary— are perceived as being of an identical nature,
how can this distinction, which arises from a single seed, belong to the others?"
It is said: Indeed, in every effect, two kinds of causes are observed—the perceived and the unperceived—and this is well-established for all who affirm the existence of all things (*sarvāstika*).
Therefore, the totality of auxiliary conditions, whether perceptible or imperceptible, cannot be apprehended through direct perception by one who is not omniscient.

Consequently, due to a specific difference in the power of the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*), there may indeed arise such a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) in certain seed-moments, by virtue of which those very seed-moments [produce] either an initial excellence or a sprout through a succession.

[Objection: "Could other seed-moments not produce [the sprout]? For, in those cases where the conditions for contact are present, is it not possible that there exists a specific distinction—characterized by the capacity to produce the initial excellence [of the series]—arising from a particularity in the power of their own causes? How can it be established that such a distinction necessarily exists therein?"
We say it is from the effect, characterized by an initial excellence, which is inferred from the arising of the sprout.
If it is argued that, because the cause is not perceived, its non-existence must follow, we reply:

no, for even when a cause consisting of a collection of both visible and invisible factors is not seen, its non-existence is not established; thus, the non-perception of the cause is of doubtful validity.
This is the meaning:

regarding the moment possessed of tactile contact, there is no difference from other moments of time that are distinct through their own differences; thus, between these two views, that one which possesses the force of valid cognition (*miti*) is the victorious one.
In that regard, for one [view], the absence of a cause is the constituent of the effect, while for the other, it is [the presence of a cause].
The causal complex, however, is not in every respect capable of being perceived, whereas the effect follows upon the means of valid cognition.

Thus, since "assistance" is not the meaning of "dependence," there is no exclusion of either [the cause or the effect] for a momentary entity even without depending on its auxiliary causes. Now, if "acting together" is the meaning of dependence, then if that depends on the qualification "of what was previously existing," such [dependence] never occurs for a momentary entity; thus, non-dependence remains unimpaired.

Now, if the meaning of "dependence" (*sāpekṣatā*) is that there is an operation [of a cause] upon that which remains already present and independent—meaning it is not dependent on what has been previously established—then there is indeed dependence and not independence.

And thus, since there is no exclusion of both [dependence and independence], the first non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). Likewise, the exclusion of the two pervaders, unity and plurality, from the momentary is also unestablished.

This is because, although there is a conceptual difference in natures such as being the material cause (*upādāna*) based on various specific exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), multiple effects are produced by a single essential nature; thus, there is no absence of both [types of] exclusion.

Furthermore, as for the argument that if the seed were a producer by means of only a single nature, then earth and the other factors would necessarily possess the nature of the sprout—otherwise, even if the cause is non-different, the difference in the effect would result in the absurdity (*prasaṅga*) of the effect being causeless—that is inconsistent.
Because the identity of the cause and the diversity of the effects are established by a clear sensory perception,
the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being produced by a single cause and being one is refuted; thus, the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is untenable.

Regarding the statement that "there is no difference in the effect when there is no difference in the cause," what is intended by "cause" here is the nature of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). The meaning is that when the causal complex is of the same genus, the effect cannot be of a different genus; however, it does not mean that a single factor within the causal complex must not produce multiple effects.
This is because the production of multiple effects from a single [complex] is established by direct perception.
Furthermore, it has already been largely established that identity cannot be proven through recognition even when there is a difference in time.

Nor has it ever been observed anywhere that sensory perception apprehends two distinct objects—one occupying a different location and the other being resistant—as being one and the same, such that a suspicion of their difference might arise even in those cases.
Moreover, if one were to entertain such a suspicion and thereby deny even clear perception, it would follow that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are abolished.
Nor is there a fallacy of doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatireka*),
because we do not accept that substances such as soil possess the nature of a seed, and because dependence upon that which provides no assistance has been refuted; thus,
it is impossible for the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) to be unestablished.
Thus, since both of these non-perceptions of pervaders (*vyāpakānupalambha*) are unestablished, existence does not exclude momentariness; therefore, this is not an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.

Furthermore, an existing entity for which the positive and negative concomitance with the probandum and its opposite is uncertain is rightly considered "uncommon," as in the case of "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*).

Moreover, due to the non-perception of the pervaders under discussion, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) itself is entirely non-existent, because it lacks a substratum, having been excluded from both [the categories] by both disputants.
So how could this [reason] be an uncommon inconclusive one? Enough with this insistence on mere prattle!

Thus, since it is impossible for that which is capable to be delayed, being the object of the conventional usage "capable" is pervaded by producing; therefore, given the existence of both the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and its contrapositive (viparyaya), the reason is not inconclusive either. Consequently, the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is established.
This is settled.
Thus, the proof of momentary destruction by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) within a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is completed.
This is the work of the great scholar Ratnakīrtipāda.
